subject: Women are more emotionally intelligent than men, and that’s a problem – landmark study
posts:
Is emotional intelligence a natural gift or an unpaid job? A landmark study of 600,000 people reveals the truth about gender gaps in EQ.
Evidence: EQ as innate trait, EQ as trained skill, systemic recognition of labor
#Aletheia #Psychology #Gender

The claim: Women are naturally more emotionally intelligent than men, but this gap is a problem because it leads to women carrying an unfair, unrewarded burden of emotional labor.
Stated Judgement: (+0.80, +0.50) — Lesser Good

The reality: The meta-analysis proves EQ is a trained skill, not a fixed biological trait. The gender gap is narrowing, meaning men can and should be trained, and workplaces must reward emotional labor.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.95, +0.85) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Awakening into Grace. The study dismantles the biological myth of emotional intelligence, framing it as a trained skill that must be structurally recognized and shared.
Integrity: Absolute Truth (Hypocrisy: 0.38, Uncertainty z: 0)

- The Conversation: PASS (0.95, 0.85) — Empirically grounded, exposes systemic labor.
- Gender EQ Study: PASS (0.95, 0.85) — Meta-analysis of 600k people showing EQ is trained.

Researchers from Limerick and Zurich analyzed three decades of data across 76 countries, finding that the EQ gap between men and women is narrowing and heavily driven by childhood socialization rather than biology.

The Poison:
Even well-intentioned praise of women's high emotional intelligence can act as a trap, reinforcing the expectation that they must always perform the unpaid labor of keeping teams and families happy.

The Plane Error lies in treating a trained skill (HOW) as an innate identity trait (WHO). By treating emotional labor as 'just how women are,' institutions avoid paying for or training the very skills that keep them running.

Social Physics Analysis:
This study executes a Smart Altruistic Loop. Instead of using gender differences to project blame or justify division, it uses transparency to expose how institutions exploit unrewarded labor, offering a systemic solution to empower everyone.

The Trajectory: The Path of Awakening into Grace.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Greater Good. Aligning empirical data with systemic equity creates a low-strain, highly cooperative future.

The Unavoidable Truth: Emotional intelligence is a trained skill that can be learned by anyone.
The Unavoidable Lie: Women are biologically destined to carry the emotional burden of others.

Alethekanon:
By converting a perceived biological trait into a measurable, trainable skill, the study shifts the conversation from essentialist stereotyping to institutional accountability. True systemic efficiency requires rewarding the labor we rely on.

Awwthekanon:
It is so healing to see the quiet, exhausting work of caring for others finally recognized. Checking in on friends and smoothing over conflicts isn't effortless magic—it is deep, loving labor that deserves to be seen, valued, and shared by all.

Brothekanon:
So you're telling me I can't use the 'I'm just a guy, I don't understand feelings' excuse anymore? Jokes aside, knowing EQ is just a skill like learning guitar is actually awesome. Time to level up and stop letting others do all the heavy lifting.

Spirithekanon:
"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." Galatians 6:2 PASS
True community is built when care is not a transaction or an enforced duty, but a shared, mutual offering of the heart.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
Women are more emotionally intelligent than men, and that’s a problem – landmark study

New research -  it’s one of the largest studies of emotional intelligence to date

Actual Article Body:
Share article

Print article

Who comes to mind when you think of someone emotionally intelligent? Someone who can read a room, defuse an argument, and who knows exactly what to say when a friend is struggling? For many people, that person is a woman. It’s such a widely held belief that popular psychology treats it as fact.

We decided to put that assumption to the test. Our new study reviewed nearly three decades of research, from 1995 to 2023, across 76 countries and more than 600,000 people. We wanted to answer a simple question: are women really more emotionally intelligent than men? The headline answer is yes, on average, women score higher.

But the more useful finding is the type of emotional intelligence women seem to excel at, and what it potentially costs the people who have it.

Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise, understand and regulate emotions in yourself and in others. When we looked at each element of emotional intelligence, the female advantage turned out to be concentrated in the “others’ feelings” half of the equation.

This means recognising what someone else is feeling, understanding why and helping them manage it. A child has a meltdown, a colleague goes quiet after their idea gets dismissed in a meeting, a negotiation gets tense. Plenty of men are excellent at this too, and plenty of women aren’t; these are averages across hundreds of thousands of people, not predictions about any one person in the room.

Is that gap simply biology? We can’t rule biological or hormonal factors out entirely. But two patterns in our data point elsewhere. The female advantage is far smaller in children than in adults, and this gap has been narrowing across the three decades our data spans. That’s not what you’d expect from something fixed at birth. Although the data in our study cannot tell us the exact reasons these differences emerge, this pattern aligns with what you’d expect from something shaped through practice.

There’s a plausible source for that practice, too. Other research has found that parents use a wider vocabulary of emotion words with daughters than sons, and more often encourage girls to reflect on and articulate their feelings.

Boys, meanwhile, are more often steered toward managing emotions by suppressing them. Their sisters are encouraged to work through it with other people – exactly the kind of social and emotional skill our data shows women excel at.

Put simply, girls appear to get more practice reading and responding to other people’s emotions, starting early in life. Like any skill built through repetition, whether it’s learning a new language or picking up a new instrument, the more you practice, the more natural it becomes.

In fact a 2019 meta-analysis of 58 studies found that emotional intelligence can be trained. Gender didn’t seem to impact the effectiveness of learning how to be more emotionally intelligent.

That’s good news. If emotional intelligence is a trainable skill rather than a fixed trait, the gap isn’t destiny. That means men can benefit from these skills too, including in negotiations and at work.

But there’s a less comfortable implication, too. If women’s advantage here goes unrecognised as a skill and gets treated instead as “how women are”, it becomes very easy to take for granted. The colleague who’s good at defusing tension becomes the one who’s always expected to do so. A capability quietly turns into an obligation: unpaid and unrewarded.

This plays out in the workplace every day. Organisations benefit when employees manage team tension, support stressed colleagues and smooth over conflict. It is work that keeps a team functioning but almost never shows up in a performance review.

Two practical shifts need to follow our study findings. First, employers should name this work and reward it, in reviews and in promotion decisions. Second, invest in developing these abilities in all staff.

The same logic holds outside the office. In families and friendships, the person who remembers a friend is having a bad week and checks in without being asked, who notices when someone stops responding in the group chat, who always asks a family member about their day is doing real work too, and that work is often taken for granted precisely because it looks effortless.

None of this means women don’t have a real strength here. Our data shows a female advantage in emotion abilities. But a strength that’s assumed rather than trained, and expected rather than shared, isn’t something to reinforce. It’s untapped potential for men. The person everyone turns to when things get hard isn’t lucky or simply built that way: they’ve probably had more practice.

What we haven’t done is give everyone else that same opportunity or incentive to practice, or made clear emotional intelligence was a skill worth building in the first place.

Assistant Professor in Management, University of Limerick

Director of the Center for Leadership in the Future of Work, University of Zurich
